angle: AI can't brainstorm from nothing. Humans bring the first 2-3 ideas and Claude gets you to 10
post_first_line: Start with 2 or 3 ideas. They have to be yours.
linkedin_post:
Start with 2 or 3 ideas. They have to be yours.

A couple weeks ago, Sarah came by our office and we ran a brainstorming session on how we can be betting more broadly as a team.

We walked through the business, every channel we run today, where we're seeing success and where we're not. We left with a bunch of ideas on how to improve what we're doing.

AI can amplify a session like that. But the kernels of insight still need to come from people.

The first 2 or 3 ideas are what give Claude something real to work with. From there, it can get you to ideas 7 through 10.

Give it nothing and you get generic output. Give it a few sharp ideas from people who know the channels and the results, and it builds on them.

So my process is simple: humans start the list, Claude extends it.

Who's doing the first draft of your brainstorms?

lesson.title: Seed the brainstorm before you hand it to AI
takeaways: AI amplifies brainstorming, but the kernels of insight still come from people.
The first 2 or 3 human ideas give Claude direction.
With that seed, Claude can help you reach ideas 7 through 10.
lesson.exercise: Before your next brainstorm, write down 2 or 3 ideas from your own experience with your channels and results. Give them to Claude as context and ask it to extend the list to 10. Compare that to a prompt with no seed ideas.

angle: Feeling behind on AI? Start with small chats, then build your first skill
post_first_line: Most people feel behind on AI.
linkedin_post:
Most people feel behind on AI.

I've watched that anxiety show up on our own team over the past few months.

The instinct is to dive into some huge, complicated use case. Don't.

Start with small chats in Claude. Then move on to building your first skill.

It doesn't need to be perfect.

The intuition comes from trying things, not from reading about them as a third party.

Nobody gets good at this by watching from the sidelines.

What's the first small thing you tried in Claude?

takeaways: Feeling behind on AI is common, and it comes from trying to figure it all out at once.

lesson.exercise: Open Claude today and run three small chats on real work you already do. Then pick one task you repeat and build your first skill for it, even if it's imperfect.

angle: Build the lead magnet, not a beautiful page: always include a CTA
post_first_line: 30 seconds to build a lead magnet page.
linkedin_post:
30 seconds to build a lead magnet page.

Sarah Charlton started with a talk to sales button, because a page like this always needs a CTA. The goal is a lead magnet, not a beautiful page.

From there, the page came together in pieces: a hero image, a fun toggle, the inputs a teammate asked for, a headline with supporting detail, and some customer quotes.

The ending matters most. Visitors can email themselves their results, and that step carries a second CTA.

Sarah called it a concept of a page. You wouldn't know from looking at it, but it took under 30 seconds to build.

When a page takes seconds to build, polish stops being the bottleneck. What the page is built to do becomes the real question.

What's the first CTA on your latest landing page?
carousel: Slide 1: This lead magnet page took under 30 seconds to build.
Slide 2: Sarah Charlton's rule: you always need a CTA.
Slide 3: The goal is a lead magnet, not a beautiful page.
Slide 4: Start with a hero image and a fun toggle.
Slide 5: Add the inputs your team actually asked for.
Slide 6: Layer in a headline, detail, and customer quotes.
Slide 7: Let visitors email themselves their results.
Slide 8: Put a second CTA at the very end.

lesson.title: Build the Lead Magnet, Not a Beautiful Page
takeaways: Every lead magnet needs a CTA. Decide on it before anything else.
Interactive elements like toggles and inputs make the page more fun to use.
Emailing results to the visitor creates a natural spot for a second CTA.
lesson.exercise: Sketch a lead magnet page on one sheet of paper. Write the top CTA, the input fields, and the post-results CTA before designing anything else.

caption: Always include a CTA

angle: We've never posted a LinkedIn post straight out of AI, and here's why
post_first_line: Zero AI-written posts. Years of LinkedIn.
linkedin_post:
Zero AI-written posts. Years of LinkedIn.

I have a specific reason for holding that line, and it's not what you'd expect.

I've written on LinkedIn for the past couple years. In that time, we have never once taken a post straight out of AI and published it.

It's just not good enough. It isn't interesting.

AI doesn't have the taste or care that someone good at marketing brings. It doesn't understand what's happening in the zeitgeist right now, or how people are feeling about things.

And I'm not confident that closing that gap is going to be quick.

So this is one area where I personally get no leverage out of it.

I'm not saying AI is useless for GTM. I use it in plenty of places. But the writing that earns attention depends on judgment about the moment, and that's still a human job.

Where has AI actually failed you in your content?

Slide 8: So here, I get no leverage from AI. Where do you?

lesson.title: Why raw AI output doesn't make good LinkedIn posts
takeaways: AI lacks the taste and care that a good marketer brings to a post.
It doesn't understand the zeitgeist or how people are feeling right now.
Knowing where AI gives you no leverage is as useful as knowing where it does.
lesson.exercise: Take your last three LinkedIn drafts and mark every line that reflects a current mood or opinion in your market. Check whether AI could have written those lines on its own.

angle: Don't ask AI to invent your ROI math. Bring the logic, let it build the page
linkedin_post:
12 pages of size 12 font.

That was the ROI calculator Sarah Charlton started with, and the way it got used is the real lesson.

Sarah Charlton was building a simplified Unify ROI calculator with Claude in a 15-minute session. The first move was not asking AI to figure out the ROI on Unify. That doesn't make sense, and it's not something to delegate.

The ROI logic came from Quentin: a detailed calculator paired with a diagram, written up as 12 pages of very detailed instructions.

That was far too much for 15 minutes. So Sarah asked Claude to make it something much simpler to build in the session.

Claude came back with a really simple calculator. That became the simplified Unify ROI calculator used for the day.

The split is clear. A human owns the math and the logic. AI handles the simplifying and the building.

Hand AI a blank page and ask it to invent your ROI, and you get numbers nobody can defend. Hand it your logic and ask it to build the page, and you get speed without losing the thinking.

Where do you draw the line with AI?

Slide 2: Sarah Charlton started with 12 pages of detailed instructions.
Slide 3: The logic came from Quentin, not from the AI.
Slide 4: With only 15 minutes, that doc was too big.
Slide 5: So Claude was asked to simplify it into something buildable.
Slide 6: The result: one simple ROI calculator, built in session.
Slide 7: Humans own the logic. AI builds the page.
Slide 8: Where do you draw the line with AI?

lesson.title: Bring the ROI logic, let AI build the page
takeaways: ROI math is not something to delegate to AI; the logic has to come from people who understand it.
A detailed source document can be too heavy for the time you have, so ask AI to simplify it.
AI is strongest at turning your logic into a simple, usable build.
lesson.exercise: Write down your ROI logic in a short doc, then ask AI to turn it into a simple one-page calculator you can use in a 15-minute session.

angle: Sales isn't AI vs. human anymore. AI is table stakes and selling stays human-to-human
post_first_line: Sarah Charlton says AI is now table stakes.
linkedin_post:
Sarah Charlton says AI is now table stakes.

The old story about AI replacing sales has quietly flipped.

A year or two ago, the debate was AI versus human. Now it's a human plus AI story.

AI should absorb the research and administration work.

Sarah's sharper take is that the best sellers think about AI as a way to get leverage. Selling itself is inherently human-to-human, and that isn't going anywhere.

So the question isn't whether to use AI. Everyone will. The edge comes from what you do with the time it gives back.

Where is AI giving you the most leverage right now?

lesson.title: Sales is human plus AI, not human versus AI
takeaways: The narrative has shifted from AI replacing sales to AI working alongside sellers.
AI should absorb research and administration work.
The best sellers use AI for leverage, while selling stays human-to-human.
lesson.exercise: List your weekly tasks and mark which are research or administration. Pick one to hand to AI this week, and spend the time saved on a direct conversation with a buyer.
